summary:
Seychelles is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016 with the repeal of Penal Code Section 151, a colonial-era provision that had carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex intimacy.

The Constitution of Seychelles guarantees freedom from torture under Article 16 and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex under Article 27. The source text listing those grounds does not name gender identity expressly.

Section 5 of the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) adds sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status to the protected characteristics, creating an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences.

The revised law increases prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward a victim's sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability. The Human Dignity Trust is cited as stating that, after South Africa, Seychelles is the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

Seychelles is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with long exposure to international visitors, and the sources reviewed record no pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
tangentialFactors:
The hate-crime provisions are reactive: they attach heavier sentences to a violent offence after the fact and do not regulate how visitors are treated in ordinary settings such as hotels, venues or transport.

The comparative standing cited by the Human Dignity Trust places Seychelles alongside South Africa as one of only two African states covering all forms of hate-based victimisation, which marks it as an outlier on the continent rather than a follower of a regional norm.

Travel and news coverage of the 2016 repeal presents the change as an opening toward LGBT visitors, and travel guidance advises visitors to stay informed about current legal and social conditions. That framing shapes expectations but is commentary, not a legal guarantee.

The constitutional protections cited are broad guarantees rather than trans-specific measures, so their practical weight for a visitor depends on how police and courts apply them.
localsOnly:
Residents of Seychelles can invoke Article 27 equal protection and the Article 16 prohibition on torture, and the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 gives prosecutors an enhanced basis to charge offences motivated by hostility toward a person's gender identity, sex characteristics or sexual orientation.

Violent crimes committed against residents on those grounds now carry increased prison sentences, and the same protected-characteristic list covers race, religion, disability and HIV/AIDS status.

The protections operate through the ordinary criminal justice system, so residents depend on police willingness to record a hate motive and on prosecutors to plead it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is not addressed in the sources reviewed; whether a trans visitor's documents can be amended, and what follows from a mismatch between passport marker and presentation, is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers are not covered by the sources reviewed, including any inspection of gender markers at arrival.

Whether the Article 27 non-discrimination grounds extend expressly to gender identity, beyond the listed ground of sex, is unresolved in the source text available.

No enforcement record for the 2024 amendments is documented: there are no reported cases, sentencing outcomes or police directives showing how the enhanced sentences have been applied.

Trans-specific facilities, healthcare access for visitors, and partner or marital recognition are not sourced in this inventory, and no crime statistics or incident reports for the country were available to test the absence of documented anti-trans violence.
